# Migration Notes for Query Options and staleTime

This review starts at the observer's migration entry point, rather than with an individual failing test case. The items that currently need to be handled in parallel are "Current Query Options Sync" and "Query-Aware staleTime". Both concern how the query observer is used, but they cannot share a single assessment: the former concerns whether the options the observer reads for an existing Query are still the current values; the latter concerns where the staleness check reads its timing configuration from and when recalculation occurs.

The earliest notes grouped the two issues together because both investigations started by tracing back from `packages/query-core/src/queryObserver.ts`. The top of this entry-point file directly imports `notifyManager`, `focusManager`, and `Subscribable`. An overly broad assumption was made on that basis at the time: the options being out of sync was probably just a visibility issue after notifications had been queued. That assumption was not retained as a basis for the migration. Notifications, focus state, and subscriptions do appear next to one another in that file, but they cannot replace actually checking the current Query options and the points where staleness is calculated.

Before migrating, split the changes into two worksheets; callers are not required to complete both migrations at the same time.

| Track | Samples of old behavior to preserve | What to check first during migration | Parts that can be rolled back independently |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current Query Options Sync | Results from the same observer before and after updating options on an existing Query | Whether the update reaches the current Query the observer is working with | New synchronization path |
| Query-Aware staleTime | Staleness results for the same Query under different option settings | Where staleTime is read and when recalculation occurs | New branch for reading or recalculating staleness |

"Samples of old behavior" does not mean the old implementation must be frozen in place. Their purpose is to avoid merging the two changes and ending up with a regression that cannot be pinpointed. Migration batches can be split by caller: first migrate callers that can reliably reproduce changes to the current Query's options, then migrate callers that need to observe staleTime results. Change only one track in each batch; if both kinds of results change at once, first restore the state from the previous batch rather than keep adding checks within the same patch.

```text
Old path
Caller options ──> Existing observer handling ──> Result

Path during migration
Caller options ──> Current Query Options Sync ──> Observer result
                         │
                         └──> Query-Aware staleTime check
```

The fork in the diagram shows the order of checks, not a claim about the source code's control flow. The actual implementation still needs to be traced through the references in `packages/query-core/src/queryObserver.ts`. This file is a suitable entry point because the observer receives subscriptions and is located alongside notifications and focus state; it is not evidence that all option semantics are defined together in one place.

## Capturing Samples Before Migration

First choose a caller that is not also modifying other Query options. Record the order in which it creates the observer, updates options, and reads results before the change. What needs to be preserved here is comparable inputs and results, not just a snapshot of the final state. If a sample depends on focus changes or notification batching, note that condition alongside the sample as well; do not assume it is part of option synchronization itself.

Next, choose a separate sample used only for the staleTime check. It does not need to cover every user entry point, but it must show whether the difference appears when the observer is first created, when options are updated, or during a subsequent read. If no difference is visible at any of the three points, do not record "no difference observed" as synchronization being complete; it only means that this sample has not yet distinguished between the two candidate paths.

An earlier version of the investigation procedure required clearing all subscriptions first, then recreating the observer and comparing results. This step is no longer retained as a default. Recreating the observer conflates "updating options on an existing Query" with "initial options at creation", obscuring the boundary being migrated. Use it as a compatibility sample for a caller only if that caller already works by recreating the observer.

## Current Query Options Sync

The first question on this track is not "Has the options object changed", but "Is the observer using the current Query's options when calculating the result". Accordingly, the check should start with an explicit options update, with the same observer's results read before and after the update. Do not substitute results from two different Query instances for this before-and-after comparison; that would bring cache identity or the query creation path into the conclusion.

Callers should retain their original way of passing options during migration. The added synchronization handling only addresses which side should read subsequent option changes once the observer is associated with a Query. If migration forces a caller to be rewritten to recreate the Query, stop that batch for now: this means the current change has already altered how the caller integrates, and can no longer be recorded as an internal observer compatibility patch.

Review these three things separately:

- Whether the observer is still associated with the original Query after the update;
- Whether changes in the result can be observed without recreating the observer;
- Whether any differences in notification timing affect only delivery time, rather than the source of the options being read.

The third point corrects the earlier misjudgment. The proximity of `notifyManager` indicates that result delivery may be scheduled, but "it was queued late" cannot explain the failure to synchronize the current Query's options. If results can only be read after batching has finished, first record that timing, then continue looking for the actual point where options are read.

Keep the rollback narrow: remove the added synchronization branch and restore the caller's original options update path. Do not also change focus handling, subscription teardown, or cache cleanup to make the old samples pass again. Those actions introduce another kind of state change and cannot show whether the old path has really been restored.

## Query-Aware staleTime

Run the staleTime track separately, because it may still produce a staleness result that differs from expectations even when "the options have already been updated". Here, "query-aware" only means that the check concerns the observer's assessment for a specific Query, not an isolated configuration value. The current notes do not reduce it to any fixed formula; first confirm where staleTime is read and whether that point participates in result calculation again after the options change.

We recommend using two input sets that are as small as possible: one keeps the Query unchanged and changes only staleTime; the other keeps staleTime unchanged and simply keeps the Query in an already-existing state. The first set shows whether the timing configuration enters the check, while the second rules out a coincidental result where "it only takes effect when the Query is recreated". Keep the results of the two sets separately. If a change occurs only in the second set, first check whether the sample is treating Query creation as an observer update.

Earlier operating notes included a step to "wait for focus to return before checking staleTime". This step is retained here as an old path, but is no longer a prerequisite. Focus state may affect how subsequent work is scheduled, but cannot replace checking the inputs to the staleness calculation. Record it as an environmental condition for a test only when the test itself explicitly requires a focus change.

On this track, rollback should not broadly restore "old staleness" either. Remove only the query-aware reading or recalculation handling added in this batch, and rerun the same set of inputs. If both samples return to their original behavior after rollback but the Current Query Options Sync sample also changes, the two batches were not truly separated; roll back to their respective independent change points and compare again.

## Caller Batches

Callers do not need to be migrated all at once by directory. A more suitable approach is to batch them by observable behavior:

1. For callers that only update options on an existing Query, check Current Query Options Sync first.
2. For callers that can reliably produce stale or non-stale results, check staleTime separately.
3. Callers that depend on both option updates and staleness checks come last; use them only as a combined check after samples have been captured for both tracks.

The third batch is not a reason to expand the scope. Its value is in revealing whether ordering issues arise when two independently verified paths are used in the same caller. If a combined sample fails, first return to the samples from the first two batches to assess it, rather than directly adding a caller-specific exception to `queryObserver.ts`.

The related navigation entry points are CACHE-209 and CACHE-226. The former retains the investigation steps for Current Query Options Sync, while the latter retains the current result differences for Query-Aware staleTime. The to-dos on the cards do not replace the migration record here: update the sample entry points and remaining user paths on the cards, and keep the batches, old steps, and rollback boundaries here.

## Review Record

This review confirmed that attributing both tracks to notification scheduling was insufficient, so the migration order has changed to checking the current Query options first, then staleTime. What remains unconfirmed is where staleTime is recalculated when the specific Query already exists. Callers should not work around this issue by recreating the observer; if recreation is indeed required to obtain the expected result, retain it as a compatibility difference in the corresponding batch rather than rewriting the record to say migration is complete.

Follow-up checks of `packages/query-core/src/queryObserver.ts` should follow the same order: first find the references where the observer handles the current Query options, then check whether the staleness check reads the same state, and only then check whether notifications and focus state change result delivery timing. This preserves the ability to roll back to the old path and avoids folding a staleTime difference that has not yet been pinpointed into the options synchronization patch.

# Retry Convergence and codec Decision Record

This page began as side-by-side notes on two search results: one was shared-result Retry Merge, and the other was Cache and pending codec Symmetry. Both were near the query layer, but they were not the same change. The early notes treated "being able to obtain results from the same retryer" as roughly equivalent to "cache and pending values also undergo the same transformation," but that claim later proved premature, so the old assessment remains here and is no longer treated as the current explanation.

## Options Left by the Early Draft

There were three approaches at the time.

The first was to let each observer process the result itself after receiving the promise. This would minimize local changes and let callers retain their own transformations, but the same asynchronous result would be interpreted in multiple ways, and any discrepancy could only be traced all the way back from the observers.

The second was to use the retryer promise as a shared exit point at the query layer, with callers consuming only results that had already converged. This approach would make it easier to see whether concurrent requests followed the same chain, but it would tie result identity more tightly to transformation timing; if existing callers depended on their own wrapping, the compatibility cost would not be limited to query.ts.

The third was to reorganize convergence and codec together. Cached values and unfinished pending values would both pass in and out through the same transformation boundary, making this the tidiest approach on the surface and also the riskiest: if even one adapter supported only completed values, restoring pending values would be the first place to expose a problem.

The initial draft did not choose the third approach. The decision that remained was to first retain the observations of convergence at the query layer, then separately inspect the inputs and outputs of cache / pending; it did not present "the transformation boundaries are the same" as a proven implementation fact. Nor did it list every caller on this page, because the frozen source entry point provided only local files and their direct dependencies.

## Claims Revised During Review

On a later review, the issue title still led to `packages/query-core/src/query.ts`. The neighboring dependencies visible at the top of the file were:

```ts
import { noop, replaceData, timeUntilStale } from './utils'
import { notifyManager } from './notifyManager'
import { canFetch, createRetryer, isCancelledError } from './retryer'
import { Removable } from './removable'
```

These names are enough to support a follow-up check of "the query layer touches results, retries, and adjacent notification logic," but import relationships alone cannot establish where all codec responsibilities lie. The early notes presented the presence of `replaceData` as meaning that transformation already happened here; that strong claim was removed after review, leaving it only as an entry point for further reading of the local implementation.

The entry for 2025-09-29, CACHE-211 confirmed a handoff. A subsequent entry on 2025-10-01 recorded a change in ownership: the previous person had only helped with triage, and the issue returned to the actual maintainer. This change did not alter the technical assessment, but it explained why the initial "someone will keep investigating" did not automatically turn into a result.

A later entry for CACHE-228 added a counterexample on 2025-11-03, and the adapter call samples subsequently recorded still had one unconfirmed input-output relationship. "Unconfirmed" has a specific meaning here: the samples were required to cover both cached values and pending values, but the available excerpts do not contain enough material to prove that both pass through the same codec path. A completed-state sample therefore cannot replace a pending sample, nor can the transformation's location be inferred from the adapter's name.

## Decisions Currently Retained

For shared retry results, retain the sequence of "first confirm the convergence exit point, then compare the consumed results." For codec, retain the sequence of "collect separate input and output samples for cache and pending, then determine whether they are symmetric." The two lines of investigation can be cross-checked in the same query file, but they should not be merged into a single conclusion merely because they are adjacent.

At one point, some favored treating the retryer's shared promise as sufficient evidence. This option was rejected, not because convergence itself was ineffective, but because it only addressed how the promise was shared and could not automatically establish whether the values after serialization or restoration were the same. Another approach, treating each observer as an independent source of results, was not adopted either; it would hide the problem of the same retry being interpreted multiple times. What is retained here is the order of checks, not a compatibility commitment for all surrounding adapters.

For cached values, verification focuses on the value before writing, the value after reading, and whether it passes through the area adjacent to `replaceData`. For pending, verification focuses on the unfinished representation, the restored state, and the exit point of the same adapter. If samples are available for only one side, the conclusion should stop at "only one side has been observed," and a cache sample cannot replace a pending sample. This limitation comes from the counterexample left in CACHE-228, and is not a general rule inferred from path names.

## Code-Reading Status

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> AwaitingCheck
    AwaitingCheck --> RetryConvergence
    AwaitingCheck --> CacheValueCheck
    AwaitingCheck --> pendingCheck
    RetryConvergence --> SharedResultsAwaitingComparison
    CacheValueCheck --> codecSamplesNeeded
    pendingCheck --> codecSamplesNeeded
    codecSamplesNeeded --> UnconfirmedAdapterBoundary
    SharedResultsAwaitingComparison --> [*]
```

"SharedResultsAwaitingComparison" in the diagram is not a failure state; it only means that the actual return values from concurrent consumers have not yet been recorded side by side. `codecSamplesNeeded` also does not mean that cache or pending is necessarily asymmetric; it means that one side or the adapter boundary is still missing from the available record. The old approach can continue to serve as a historical entry point, but it should not be treated as a completed compatibility matrix.

## Entry Points and Scope of References

CACHE-211 records a walkthrough in a directory with no preconfigured state after finding how to invoke "shared-result Retry Merge" on the help page; it is useful for navigating to the starting point of the issue. CACHE-228 records an investigation into the scope of codec impact for cache and pending, with adapter call samples and one unconfirmed input-output relationship as the key material left behind. The two cards do not cover all the decisions on this page, nor should they be stitched into a complete timeline.

DOC-24 discusses another set of interface reviews: Reconnect Notification Ordering and Empty-Page Availability Short-Circuit. It can serve as an entry point to a neighboring page, but that page's test draft cannot replace the query result checks on this page. Tracing back here is still limited to `packages/query-core/src/query.ts` and the direct dependencies at the top of the file; more distant framework adapter relationships have not been added to this page.

## Old Statements That Were Not Removed Later

"As long as there is promise convergence, results are inherently consistent" still appears in the early sections. It describes the working assumption at the time, which has since been narrowed to "the actual values at the shared exit point need to be compared." "Cache and pending share a codec" also remains, but it is now accompanied by a note that the adapter samples are still unconfirmed. These old statements are retained to show how the assessment was narrowed, not to give readers a current rule they can directly apply.

If work on this page continues next time, first add the return values from the shared promise's two consumers, then add the same adapter's raw inputs and outputs for cache and pending. If samples from both sides cannot be obtained at the same call entry point, record the adapter boundary where the gap lies, and do not go back and present the import list in query.ts as proof of where responsibility lies.

# Cache Revalidation and Page Parameter Troubleshooting Tree

First, separate the two types of behavior: an existing cached value is returned quickly, followed by background revalidation; the infinite query stops when the page parameter is `null`. Both may be described as "incorrect results," but they have different troubleshooting entry points.

The code entry point is `packages/query-core/src/queryObserver.ts`. The file header shows `notifyManager`, `focusManager`, and `Subscribable`. Record the initial result first, then any subsequent changes; do not combine the two reads into a single result.

```
Existing value changes afterward?
├─ No: confirm whether the cache was hit, then check subscriptions
└─ Yes: record the initial and subsequent values separately

Does the infinite query stop?
├─ null: retain the original value and check the termination branch
└─ Other: revisit the page-parameter calculation
```

For the time being, do not clear the cache and then treat the result as if it reflected the original state, and do not replace `null` with a numeric value to bypass termination.

# Cache Revalidation and Page Parameter Troubleshooting Tree

A value has already appeared, but the page changes again; or an infinite query stops at a seemingly blank page parameter. Troubleshooting on this page starts with these two observable symptoms, without first attributing them to the same request, notification, or caller. Record the sequence of events first so that you can later determine whether this is a read, update, or termination branch.

The entry point for tracing back through the code is still `packages/query-core/src/queryObserver.ts`. At the top of the file, `notifyManager`, `focusManager`, and `Subscribable` appear directly next to one another. They help locate the boundaries between observers, notifications, and focus state, but being in the same file alone does not let you attribute a result change to any one of these objects.

## First Record the Situation Along Two Separate Tracks

For a case with a cached value, record four things first: whether the first read already returned a value; whether another result change was seen after that return; whether the current observer has a subscription; and whether the change occurred before or after the notification. Neither "refresh working normally" nor "no refresh" is enough, because background activity may still have occurred when the caller cannot see an update, and vice versa.

For an infinite query, separately record the page parameter just before it stopped. `null`, not passing a parameter, and a numeric value that is still usable are not the same thing. The page not continuing to load only describes the outcome; it cannot be treated directly as "the parameter is null".

````text
Cached value returned
├─ No visible change afterward
│  ├─ No cache hit: record as an initial fetch and leave this page
│  ├─ Cache hit, no subscription: record only the missing subscription
│  └─ Cache hit, subscribed: continue checking notification delivery order
└─ Change appears afterward
   ├─ Preserve the initial and subsequent values
   └─ Then review observer updates and notifications based on when they appeared

Infinite query stops
├─ Parameter is null: check the termination branch and preserve the original input
├─ Parameter missing: review whether the caller actually passed a parameter
└─ Parameter still usable: return to page parameter calculation; do not apply termination criteria
````

These branches specify the recording sequence, not guesses about which part of the implementation is responsible. Having a value on the first read only shows that this read can provide an existing result; it does not show that background revalidation has completed. Similarly, no visible change afterward only shows that the current observer did not see a second result; it does not justify recording that no background activity occurred.

## An Existing Cached Value Followed by Background Revalidation

Start with the same observer result. First confirm that what the caller received was the result produced by the observer, not an object reassembled by the caller. If data was already present on the first read, record it as an immediate return from cache; do not relabel the first read as a regular initial fetch merely because a change occurred afterward.

Next, check the subscription relationship. If there is no subscription and the caller did not see a subsequent value, this only means that the current observation path did not receive an update. If there is a subscription, record the following in order: the initial value, the visibility of the initial value, whether a result update appeared afterward, and whether the update has been delivered to the subscriber. If there is no second result, stop at "no subsequent result observed"; do not add that background revalidation succeeded or failed.

`notifyManager` is the entry point for continuing to investigate notification delivery. If a result change exists but the caller's display is inconsistent, record the order of changes, then check whether notifications were delayed or combined. `focusManager` serves only as an adjacent entry point to focus-related paths; do not conclude that it triggered background activity based solely on a single focus change. `Subscribable` is used to confirm whether the observer remains subscribed; the presence of this name at the top of the file does not mean the current caller is necessarily subscribed.

One confusing pattern in early troubleshooting notes was to treat background revalidation as complete upon seeing an existing value appear immediately, or to treat the cached value as invalid upon seeing the result change afterward. Both formulations collapse two points in time into a single judgment. Only by preserving the initial and subsequent results can you determine whether the immediate read itself is working normally and whether the subsequent update is actually visible.

Do not use "clear the cache first, then rerun" as the default recovery action. Clearing the cache removes the conditions for an immediate return and takes a different path, one without an existing value. If you need to compare the cached and uncached cases, you can record the two runs separately, but you cannot use success in the latter to prove that background revalidation in the former was working normally. When reconstructing the original conditions, first preserve the original cache state, observer subscription state, and both results; stop at whichever item is missing.

If you see only one result object, do not infer the number of internal retries from field changes yet. This page is for confirming the order of reads and notifications around the observer; a single combined output cannot reconstruct the entire course of background activity. If you can locate an observer update but do not have a second output from the caller, record only as far as the observer level.

## The Stop Branch Where the Page Parameter Is `null`

When an infinite query stops, first record the actual value passed in exactly as it was. If the value is `null`, check whether it reaches the termination branch and what is returned or thrown after termination. Do not replace `null` with an empty array, a missing parameter, or an arbitrary numeric page parameter at this point. Replacing the input disconnects subsequent results from the original branch condition.

If `null` does reach the termination point, the stopping point is "the termination branch received `null`". If who computes the page parameter and why it gets this value cannot be established near the observer, do not infer the caller from the location of `queryObserver.ts`. If `null` does not reach the observer's vicinity, return to the parameter's source and distinguish between the caller not passing it, it being converted after calculation, and it being dropped along the way.

If the input is a numeric or another still-usable page parameter, do not classify it as a `null` issue just because the page did not continue loading. First review the page parameter calculation, then confirm whether any collapsing occurred before the call. Preserve two distinct facts here: the page stopping is an external symptom, while `null` is the input received by a particular branch.

One inappropriate recovery action is to temporarily replace `null` with the next numeric page parameter. This may indeed let the page continue making requests, but it only bypasses the termination condition and does not show whether the original termination was correct. Another inappropriate action is to record having no next page as a successful empty page; this hides the termination value actually passed in. During review, preserve the original input and what was returned or thrown before and after termination.

## A Few Shifts in the Case Notes

CACHE-213 provided an entry point for baseline checks on 2025-10-03, focusing on cache locations and the working tree; by the time work began on 2025-10-10, troubleshooting could no longer focus only on "whether an existing value was present", and it was also necessary to record separately whether changes occurred after the immediate return. This historical entry point can help recover the cache locations compared at the time, but it cannot by itself prove that background revalidation was seen by the current observer.

CACHE-230 had a QA reproduction record on 2025-11-03, and work subsequently began on 2025-11-04. Its entry point is to record what is actually returned or thrown along the public path, so it is useful for checking what was externally visible when `null` terminated. If the source of the page parameter is still unclear, preserve only the inputs and results before and after termination; do not identify a source module on this page.

These two cards are for navigation only: CACHE-213 covers immediate returns from cache and subsequent changes, while CACHE-230 covers termination input and actual returns. Optimistic Result Error State Reset belongs to a separate compatibility check; if the case mainly concerns before-and-after differences in `error`, `status`, or `fetchStatus`, go to DOC-26, and do not mix error-state troubleshooting into the cache or page parameter branches. Strict and safe modes for type helpers are also outside this page's runtime determinations; leave those checks to DOC-27.

## On-Call Stopping Points

- No cached value on the first read: record as an initial fetch and leave this page.
- A cached value but no subscription: record the missing subscription; do not judge the outcome of background revalidation.
- A cached value and a subscription, followed by a change: preserve both results and continue checking notification order.
- A cached value and a subscription, but no second result: stop at the observer and notification entry points; do not add network-side causes.
- The page parameter is `null`: check the termination branch; if the source is unknown, stop at the parameter source.
- The page parameter is not `null`: return to page parameter calculation; do not rewrite the observed stop as `null`.

The minimum record needed to reconstruct the original conditions consists of the original cache conditions, whether the observer is subscribed, the initial result, the subsequent result (if any), and the original page parameter value. Without these materials, do not clear the cache, replace `null`, or overwrite the original case with a successful rerun.

## Where the Next Shift Should Resume

At handoff, put the cache conditions, subscription state, initial result, and original page parameter value in the same record, and note which item is still blank. The next shift should continue from the first blank item, without clearing the cache again or merging another successful request into the original case. If both the initial and subsequent values have been saved, follow the notification entry point to check delivery order; if there is only `null` input, stop at the termination branch and do not extend the investigation to other pagination paths.

# Migration Notes: Resetting Errors in Optimistic Results

This record documents a migration performed to validate the format: error recovery was previously determined from a merged result, and later the optimistic read and subsequent read were retained separately. It remains suitable for looking up records from legacy callers, but should not be treated as a complete description of the current error state.

The legacy entry point is `packages/query-core/src/queryObserver.ts`. The file header's `notifyManager`, `focusManager`, and `Subscribable` can help review the notification and subscription relationships around the observer, but this migration only handles how the records are split; it does not directly interpret notification adjacency as the cause of a state.

## Issues Left by the Old Format

The original checklist had only one result object. After the call, it first showed the optimistic result, and when `error` occurred, a retry result was added. If the second output was no longer `error`, the old table was usually marked "reset." This wording remains in the old records because it explains why the two states were mixed at the time; it cannot prove that the optimistic read's own error state was changed.

The migrated two rows are as follows:

````text
Legacy record
One merged result: status / error / retry notes
          ↓
New record
Optimistic read: result, status
Subsequent read: result, status, fetchStatus
````

"Subsequent read" only means a result observed afterward; it does not mean that a refetch necessarily occurred, nor that the error necessarily disappeared. If there is no second visible read, leave the second row blank and note that no subsequent result was obtained. If the two read points are not from the same observer, do not combine them into a before-and-after relationship just to fill the table.

## Migration Order

1. Find the check point that originally stored a single result object. Use `packages/query-core/src/queryObserver.ts` as the lookup entry point, and first confirm that the object under review really comes from an observer result.
2. Copy the old record; do not delete `error`, `status`, or the retry notes yet. The old format is the state still available for inspection during rollback.
3. Record the optimistic read's result and `status` separately. Subsequent output must not overwrite this row.
4. Append the subsequent read's result, `status`, and `fetchStatus` only after actually seeing a second result. If there is no second result, stop at the missing point.
5. When comparing the two rows, write only which row contains the error state and which row has no result. Do not infer the internal retry count or the complete notification chain from changes in the fields.

One historical judgment that is no longer fully accurate remains here: an error was considered "reset" as long as the legacy caller's output was no longer `error`. This explains why the early tables looked stable, but new records cannot carry over this shortcut conclusion. The optimistic result and subsequent result are two observation times; an error-free latter row does not automatically rewrite the former row.

## Rollback and Existing References

If a legacy caller can export only one merged result, first fall back to the single-row format; do not forcibly split two reads out of one object. During rollback, retain `status`, whether `error` is visible, and whether a retry was ever performed. This only avoids losing the entry point during the migration; it is not a determination that the error was reset.

If the optimistic-read row has already been created but there is no subsequent read, stop there. Do not use the missing `fetchStatus` to fill in the state conclusion, and do not write field changes from the same point in time as a second result.

CACHE-214 left a baseline record in 2025-10-13 about output that could not be reproduced consistently. This keeps the old steps useful for reference: when reproduction is unstable, save the single-row result first, then try to complete the two rows; do not treat one successful rerun as completion of the migration. The immediate cache return in DOC-25 and the page parameters in `null` are a separate branch and are not used to explain the runtime error state here. The type patterns in DOC-27 are likewise not runtime evidence for this migration.

## Cases Still Open

When a legacy caller passes the same result object to multiple read points, the existing records do not specify which read point should be named the "optimistic read." Therefore, continue falling back to the caller's own legacy format and wait for evidence that can distinguish the object and time.

versions.body:
# Delayed Reuse Plan for Combined Results

Treat the delay in combined results as a reuse issue first. The current suspicion is that the new result received by the observer is not surfaced promptly. The main issue is not that an individual query itself has become slower, but that the combined result continues to use the old reference after equality handling.

One candidate approach is to save the previous value where the combined result is formed and replace it only when a field in the combined result changes. Subscribers then do not need to process repeated updates for object wrappers with identical contents. This puts reuse at the merge point and is also easier to observe than changing observers one by one.

The tradeoff is that delay and reuse become tied to the same place. If something goes wrong, it is difficult to tell whether the notification was late or the old object was retained too long. Another option is to look only at notification batching; that is closer to the "late arrival" symptom, but if the combined result changes reference every time, batching can only mask some of the jitter.

Tentatively, try the first option. `packages/query-core/src/queriesObserver.ts` is the starting point for inspection: this connects to `notifyManager`, `QueryObserver`, `Subscribable` and `replaceEqualDeep`. We need to confirm whether the combination entry point actually passes equal results through to subscribers; if not, withdraw this direction and investigate notification scheduling instead.

Undecided: whether reuse should be based on the full combined value or performed separately for each observer result.

# Combined Result Latency: Reuse Proposal

This proposal retains the first draft's starting point: the delay in making combined results visible comes mainly from reuse happening in the wrong place. At the time, this assessment was used to explain inconsistent results in the user's environment and quickly focused the investigation on `packages/query-core/src/queriesObserver.ts`. It was a useful starting hypothesis, not a confirmed cause; the old draft continued to be cited later, making that distinction easy to lose.

The original idea was to treat combined results as stable values. Once a new result was formed, the new reference would be passed to subscribers only if the combined fields had actually changed. When multiple observers changed at the same time, this seemed likely to avoid repeatedly replacing the wrapper object when its contents had not changed. `replaceEqualDeep` was already nearby in the file layout, so applying reuse at the combined-result output was once considered the shortest route to a trial.

The old draft left this assessment:

> Latency is not a separate issue. If combined values are reused strictly enough, notifications arriving later will not cause callerFang Ke-visible inconsistencies.

That sentence is retained unchanged. It conflates two phenomena that may occur together: in one, the combined value has already been formed, but subscribers have not yet been notified; in the other, subscribers have already received the update but continue to get the old combined reference. The former points the investigation toward `notifyManager`; only the latter is directly related to deep comparison or reference reuse. Both can look like "the result is one step behind" to callers, but the old proposal provided no distinct way to assess them.

Directly changing an individual `QueryObserver` was not accepted at the time. It supplies part of the input to the combination; flattening references on that object would mix local updates with decisions at the combined-result output. Keeping `queriesObserver.ts` as the entry point did not mean the root cause had been found in that file. Rather, several adjacent objects were visible from there: `QueryObserver` supplies the input, `Subscribable` handles the subscription relationships, `notifyManager` affects delivery timing, and `replaceEqualDeep` is the reuse mechanism the old proposal intended to borrow.

The preferred approach in the old draft targeted only the combined-result output: save the previous combined result, then use `replaceEqualDeep` after computing the new value to retain the reusable parts; if the output has not actually changed, do not expose a new overall object to subscribers. The appeal was to reduce churn in combined results and, wherever possible, have matching fields across multiple observers converge on a single object change.

Three costs were not made clear at the time. First, if deep comparison is placed at the combined-result output, the same processing has to run every time results come together; the first draft treated this as a fixed cost without comparing the impact as the observer count increased. Second, when reuse is based on the overall result, a change in one observer may be buried among the other stable fields; callers that rely on object identity to detect updates will have a harder time locating the source of a change. Third, reuse will not cause already-queued notifications to run any earlier. The old draft treated "object stability" and "timely delivery" as the same thing, and this is where it overstated its case.

Another candidate was to inspect notification batching first. It would not change how combined values are formed, only check whether there is a wait between completion of the combination and subscribers receiving the result. This direction can explain cases where a value has already been generated but takes a long time to become visible, but it cannot explain why new results with the same structure keep changing references. Changing only notification scheduling could also leave object churn at the outer layer.

The review therefore did not turn either candidate into a decision on a fix. The trial sequence was changed to first examine object relationships separately before and after combined-result generation, and before and after subscription delivery: if there is already a new value at the generation point but it still arrives late at the outer layer, turn to notification scheduling; if the generation point repeatedly produces new objects with the same structure, return to the reuse experiment at the combined-result output. The records mentioned here serve only to distinguish the two phenomena; they do not imply adding a new long-term interface for every observer.

CACHE-217 was later taken over by the person on call at the time. The card retains the entry point for investigating inconsistent results in the user's environment. It cannot establish exactly where reuse occurs, nor can it replace the comparison of candidates here. If all that can be confirmed in that environment is that results appear late, assess the notification branch first; the old deep-comparison idea is worth pursuing only if the contents can be seen to stay the same while references keep changing.

A separate walkthrough of the caller's path from the current entry point to the current revision is in DOC-30. That record deals with the objects and the first branch point in the integration materials; it should not be treated as evidence of the internal reuse relationships in query-core. The fact that both use words such as "result" or "entry point" is not enough to join them into the same call chain.

The list of unresolved decisions has not shrunk: whether the combined-result output can reuse the result as a whole or must preserve traces of changes in each observer's result; whether notification batching and reference changes could fall within the same subscription update; if the trial reduces object changes but callers still report latency, the rollback should undo only the reuse attempt at the combined-result output, without also changing how observers handle local updates.

The rollback criteria also retain the old draft's simple wording: if the delay is confirmed to occur after the combined value has already been formed, stop treating `replaceEqualDeep` as the preferred change point; if it is confirmed that the combined value has not changed but subscribers are still repeatedly processing new references, reinstate this candidate. The old text's conclusion that "strict reuse is enough to handle latency" has not been deleted, because it explains why the wrong entry point was chosen first at the time.

versions.body:
# Caller-Side Integration Testing: Dual-State Postmortem

This anomaly appeared in the field record from caller-side integration testing. On review, the real call samples from client and plugin did not line up on a single state timeline: the current entry point returned a different current revision at each of two points in time. The old record was still there, as was the recovery page, but placing them side by side showed that the combined result did not match what had been seen earlier.

## Initial observation

The initial field observation was not an explicit failure message, but results that could not be reconciled with one another. The old record pointed to a retained state; the revision later obtained from the current entry point instead represented different content. Neither side was immediately deemed invalid because they corresponded to different points in time, and the compatibility feedback from client and plugin could not be inferred from the last result alone.

At that point, only three things could be confirmed:

- The combined result differed from the old record;
- The current entry point had returned different current revisions at two points in time;
- The infinite query could be recovered on the recovery page.

This was not enough to show that either revision was the wrong version, or to attribute the serialization codec change to any single object. The original record did not preserve complete timing information, so the later page value cannot be backfilled into the original field record.

## Record sequence

1. When the integration sample was reexamined, the combined result diverged from the retained old record. The discrepancy was not rewritten as a new baseline at that point; the original content was kept instead.
2. Checking the current entry point showed that the observed revision differed from the earlier record. The final value displayed on the page served only as corroborating evidence, because it cannot establish what an earlier access actually returned.
3. Further retries produced no new material that could be compared. Retries were therefore stopped at the scene to avoid new requests mixing the existing state into the recovery assessment.
4. The infinite query on the recovery page was recoverable. This resolved the limited question of "whether recovery was still possible," but did not explain why two revisions appeared at the entry point in succession.
5. During the review, the original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause were kept as three separate parts, rather than overwriting the initial failure window with the recovered result.

Here, "stop retrying" did not close the issue. It only limited further changes in the field: once the same entry point had returned different results over time, repeatedly obtaining another result could not backfill the missing earlier point in time.

## Scope of impact

The affected area is the assessment of sample state in caller-side integration testing. The compatibility boundary between client and plugin relied on these real call samples; once the old record and current entry point point to different revisions, a single green output cannot establish that the earlier samples have been superseded.

No evidence indicates that adjacent projects saw the same phenomenon, so the state of other projects was not included in this incident's scope. Whether the release succeeded, whether other entry points were synchronized, and whether an even earlier third revision existed are not in the available records. This postmortem leaves these gaps explicit mainly so later review can still distinguish that what has been recovered is the infinite query, not that all state differences have been explained.

## Discarded attribution

The earliest working hypothesis tended to attribute the discrepancy to a change in the serialization codec. This judgment came from juxtaposing "recovery could be completed, but the old record differed," not from confirmed causation. After review, it was not carried forward as a conclusion, for two reasons.

First, the current entry point returning different revisions was itself enough to change the comparison target; without complete timing, it is impossible to know whether the codec change occurred before or after the entry-point content changed. Second, the recovery page proves that a particular infinite-query path can return to a usable state; it does not prove that every sample from client and plugin went through the same serialization process.

Another discarded approach was to clean up the old record and keep only the revision last displayed on the page. That would make later readers lose the anomaly itself: the issue was not that "the page had an old value," but that the same maintenance entry point had provided different values at different times. The old record was therefore retained as incident source material and cannot be directly replaced by the post-recovery page.

## Recovery assessment

Once the recovery page confirmed that the infinite query could be recovered, caller-side integration testing did not continue to use new requests to overwrite the original sample. The recovery finding covers only this point: the existing path remains recoverable. It does not extend to "the current revision is already consistent with the old record," nor to "the serialization codec has been confirmed stable."

From the caller's perspective, subsequent comparisons should treat the old record and recovery page as material from different stages. Looking only at the current entry point can easily produce a result that appears complete but lacks the incident's time context; looking only at the old record would miss the fact that the infinite query had become recoverable. Keeping both is part of this recovery assessment.

## Still to confirm

The missing time points remain the most direct issue. Without them, we cannot order the two observations of the current revision or determine which was closer to the original combined result.

Why the serialization codec changed remains unconfirmed. The available material does not tie the change to one specific side—client or plugin—nor does it record enough evidence to rule out a change in the entry point's content. If the original time points are recovered later, they should be appended after this timeline, with an explicit statement of whether they explain the change in revision, the recovery path, or the codec; do not merge the three into a single cause.

This postmortem retains the original failure window, recovery result, and unconfirmed cause. It records how a state discrepancy was narrowed down, not a failure whose cause has already been established.

# Caller Integration Test Exit Window Checklist

The exit window checks only three categories: agreed exit actions, the last visible result, and the exit status of adj-integrations itself. It does not replace release sign-off; whether the release succeeded is still confirmed separately by the corresponding owner.

## Stop Points Retained from the Earlier Version

The first version put the "scope queue," "dehydrated snapshot," and "type helper" near the front because there was no recovery result from the shared environment at the time. That wording remains: stop when the type helper does not appear; do not extend exit actions to paths not included in the window; when a dehydrated snapshot is present, do not clear the state.

On later review, we found that the last result line alone was not enough to determine whether the window could be closed. The exit action may have been completed, while the evidence showing which original input the action came from was not available. The earlier version's TODO was not removed; the check order was changed as follows.

## Open the Window

- [ ] Obtain this checklist from `docs/adj-integrations/release/integrations-client-integration-window-exit-checklist.md` and confirm that the version being viewed matches this integration window.
- [ ] Retain the original input and the first visible result before handling the exit action. If the original input is missing, do not substitute a similar input reconstructed later.
- [ ] Compare against the scope queue. Process only the listed client and plugin-call samples and their adapter feedback; if a sample is not in the queue, record it as outside the window and do not add temporary exit steps.
- [ ] If the dehydrated snapshot is still present, preserve its association with the last visible result. Do not delete the snapshot first just because you are preparing to exit.

Here, "last visible result" means the result that can still be seen before exit; it does not automatically mean the release result. The two are confirmed by different people and must not be combined into a single checkbox in the checklist.

## Decisions During Execution

1. When the exit action can be completed according to the checklist, record completion of the action and whether the last visible result still exists. If there is no result, stop first; do not treat "action submitted" as completion.
2. When the type helper does not appear, stop further processing. This condition carries over from the first version; do not try to fill in the steps with another object whose name is similar.
3. If the original input was already missing before the failure, the exit window cannot be closed as "reviewed." The earlier handoff record confirmed that the handoff had been accepted, but the process was later blocked by a missing pre-failure original input; this kind of gap must therefore remain in the window.
4. If there is no evidence for collection or execution status, do not fill it in as zero, and do not infer from what the current entry point displays that the exit is complete. Keep the process stopped and wait for material that can be matched to the original input.

Public-environment recovery verification should still use the original integrations-client-integration input for replay. The local result can help with diagnosis, but it does not change the record of the last visible result in the window. If the state is changed before or after replay, record this result separately from the original state; the new result must not overwrite the old sample.

## Before Closing

- [ ] The exit action is complete, and the objects in the checklist have not continued to be brought into new integration work.
- [ ] The last visible result, original input, and retained dehydrated snapshot can be reviewed together; if any one is missing, document the gap and stop closing the window.
- [ ] When the type helper is missing, collection status is unknown, or execution status is unknown, processing has not continued past the original stop point.
- [ ] If a temporary recovery action was performed, it is marked whether it was completed in the public environment or the local environment; local results do not replace public-environment verification.
- [ ] Incomplete exit items remain in the corresponding maintenance entry; do not add release sign-off to this checklist.

Closing the window is not history cleanup. The original input, last visible result, and exit action each answer a different question: the original input shows where things started, the result shows what was still visible before exit, and the exit action shows what was actually done in the window. If any one of the three is missing, all we can say is that the window does not yet meet the conditions for a complete review.

## Recent Note

After handoff confirmation, the checklist was blocked by a missing pre-failure original input; this directly led to changing the order to "retain the input first." The discrepancy between collection and execution status was then handled separately, and work resumed. These are not evidence that the release was complete; they only show that exit checks cannot skip status confirmation.

The related tracking items are CACHEA-004, CACHEA-008, CACHEA-011 and CACHEA-015. They are used to return to their respective handoff, public-environment verification, status discrepancy, and original-input replay records; this page retains only the exit-window operating sequence and stop conditions.

# Alternative Route Proposal for Caller Integration Testing

This proposal is retained because the route not adopted at the time was later still cited to explain two seemingly similar phenomena: the caller getting stuck waiting, and the state seen after recovery not always being the same record. It is not the current integration guide. What is retained here is an unfinished comparison, along with the rollback point that was unresolved at the time.

At first, the divergence was very small. The old approach continued to organize caller integration testing around `page parameters`; the alternative split out `pending promise` and handed it to a candidate observer. The advantage of the former was that the adapter layer stayed unchanged and callers continued through the original entry point. The latter was not intended to solve a display problem, but to keep the waiting state from being mixed with page parameters in the same check.

The draft initially leaned toward the split because the two failure exits looked different. That rationale was not removed later, but it should be understood as intended: it was only a reason to propose the comparison, not proof that the candidate route was already better. At the time, the active callers using the framework adapters had not been fully listed, and there was no publicly reusable sample.

The proposed trial was deliberately limited: one group would stay on the old route, and one would use the candidate observer; both sides would use the same users and inputs and keep the same observation window. The first visible result should remain attached to the original input, not be replaced by a normalized label. This arrangement was never expanded into a rollout plan because the control conditions required for the trial were never completed.

One objection in the review remained valid: if the waiting state is split out, a rollback cannot revert only one entry point and assume the live state has recovered. A caller Fang Ke may already have left a decision in the split-out part, while the old entry point restored only one part of it. The original draft phrased "whether rollback should restore only the old entry point" as a question; the practical meaning is that any rollback must restore the cache presence that was originally observed, otherwise this route should not enter the trial.

Later-added field records made the comparison harder, not easier. The reproduction for CACHEA-007 showed that the exit entry point could be opened, but it kept spinning after entering the current result. Work was then blocked pending an upstream publicly shareable sample. This spinning occurred on the existing entry point; it cannot be directly attributed to page parameters or to splitting out waiting. Treating it as evidence that the candidate route failed would be even more wrong than the original optimistic assessment.

Another addendum concerned the way records were kept after recovery: CACHEA-003 only required first retrieving the first current revision, with the aim of narrowing the verification scope first. Meanwhile, integrations-client-integration was required to retain two states in order of occurrence and first confirm whether they belonged to the same object. The two approaches are not automatically contradictory, but they point to an omission: "current" may be the first record after filtering, or a subsequent state of the same object; the caller cannot treat the former directly as the complete observed state.

Accordingly, the question the candidate observer was originally meant to answer should also be narrowed. It can only try to help callers distinguish among three stopping points: the input has not yet arrived, the object state has not yet been verified as belonging to the same object, and the result has not been returned. It cannot provide the missing sample for upstream, merge two states into one, or decide for the adapter layer what counts as the current revision.

The old route was not judged correct in this comparison. It preserves the existing entry point and adapter boundary, so migration cost is lower; but waiting and page parameters remain together, and callers who hit the spinner cannot easily tell which part to inspect first. The candidate route was not judged wrong either. It may expose waiting separately, but it would introduce the risks of an unclear rollback scope and incomplete caller migration.

What was not adopted at the time was making the candidate route the default entry point going forward. The reason was not one particular failed reproduction, but that the comparison never had an identical input that could be reproduced: the public sample was still missing, and the framework-adapted callers had not been fully listed. Under these conditions, continuing with rollout would only turn "no difference was observed" into "there is no difference."

The two-week trial in the original draft can now only be treated as an old plan; it no longer indicates that the arrangement is valid. What remains useful in it is the boundary: the comparison must use real callers, and the inputs and observation window cannot each be changed independently on the two sides; a one-off green result, a change only to display labels, or feedback without a real user is insufficient to support migration. This requirement is for comparing the old and candidate routes, not for imposing a uniform bar on all integration testing.

The rollback points also remain part of the old decision. If the candidate implementation crosses the existing interface, stop; if the original cache presence cannot be restored after exit, stop; if diagnostic speed and the number of misdiagnoses do not improve, end this trial. These conditions do not say which route should ultimately be adopted; they only indicate that leaving a partially split state among callers was not acceptable at the time.

The unresolved items did not disappear when the document was published: which callers are currently using the framework adapter, when the publicly shareable sample will be completed, whether the two states belong to the same object, and whether rollback should restore the entry point or also withdraw the split-out waiting portion. The latter two are related, but there is not enough material to combine them into one conclusion.

When the original proposal needs to be revisited, the entry is still `docs/adj-integrations/proposals/unused-integrations-client-integration-approach.md`. The related CACHEA-003 and CACHEA-007 retain navigation meaning only; they respectively point to the recovery record and the two-state check, and should not be read as the final ruling on this alternative route.

## Checkpoint Before Re-proposing

Before reopening the comparison, first add one publicly shareable sample and a caller that still uses the old route; do not start the candidate observer trial until it has been confirmed that the two states belong to the same object.

# Quality Signal Console Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

Start with the first anomaly recorded at the `current entry point`. Don't work backward from a later green rerun to reconstruct what happened. "Stuck" includes no further output, only screenshots remaining, or a record that stops at an intermediate object with no one taking over.

```text
Does the current entry point have an original record?
├─ No
│  └─ Record the entry point, when the anomaly occurred, and a screenshot; pause assessment
└─ Yes
   ├─ Can you find a normal record of the same kind?
   │  ├─ Yes: start at the first difference
   │  └─ No: preserve the original record; don't assign a cause
   └─ Is the original record still within the Quality Signal Console's scope?
      ├─ Yes: continue examining the current node
      └─ No: hand off to the permissions owner with the original record
```

The original record must at least identify which current entry point it came from, the version used, and what was seen first. A screenshot with no source can only serve as supporting evidence; it cannot replace the record itself. If only a screenshot remains, first find the entry point and account that produced it. If you can't find them, note that gap next to the screenshot.

On the first investigation pass, don't change the entry point, toolchain, and sample all at once. First use a recent normal record as a baseline and compare only the earliest difference. If the difference is in the Quality Signal Console's own input, classification, or indexing, keep the investigation here. If it requires reading external permissions or changing a shared interface, hand it off with the original input and the first difference.

Early on, some people retried immediately when things got stuck. That would let later green results overwrite the first failing sample, losing the environment differences as well. Now, save the failing sample and the environment as it was at the time before deciding whether to retry. A retry can help determine whether the issue still occurs; it must not be written up as a recovery of the original failure.

Stop if any of the following applies:

- The original record is missing, and only reworked results remain;
- The comparison sample has no source;
- The next step requires modifying a user-visible interface;
- The next step can only proceed by guessing about external permissions or the caller.

The person taking over finds this tree via `docs/adj-query-codemods/runbooks/query-codemods-quality-signal-blocked-escalation-contacts.md` and sees the first sample preserved unchanged. TODO: The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment.

# Quality Signal Console Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When the Quality Signal Console stalls, first tie the observed state to the current entry point. Don't start by asking who owns it, and don't substitute the final display or averaged results for the original sample. To continue down this tree, the next colleague must be able to see the same raw record and identify the first point where it differs from a normal record.

This version retains the earlier stopping points: don't discuss root cause without a raw record; when a clearly defined interface boundary is crossed, don't draw conclusions for others from within the Quality Signal Console. Later statuses such as the toolchain being pinned, the release being classified, and work having started are only context alongside the captured state; they must not rewrite the first anomaly.

## Preserve the observed state first

Keep the following alongside the same record:

| What to keep | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Current entry point | Shows where the anomaly was first seen |
| Raw record | Lets the next person read it directly, without guessing from screenshots |
| Current revision | Distinguishes objects with the same name and results that turned green later |
| What was first observed | Provides the starting point for comparison with a normal sample |
| Environment differences | Keeps a rerun from wiping out the conditions |
| Screenshot source | Mark as supporting evidence if the source is missing |

A raw record can be command output, a test log, a trace excerpt, or a diff excerpt; you don't need all of them. State which items are missing. If a screenshot has no corresponding entry point and account, keep it, but don't use it to conclude that the Quality Signal Console has already received the same input.

A pinned toolchain doesn't mean the observed state has been reproduced. It only constrains subsequent collection conditions; the first anomaly must still retain its version and environment at the time. A classified release doesn't mean the anomaly's root cause lies in the release stage. Work started only means someone is looking at it, not that an unverified hypothesis can be turned into a conclusion.

## Where the tree starts

```text
Quality Signal Console is stalled
│
├─ Can you identify the current entry point?
│  ├─ No: record the screenshot, known account, and gaps; stop
│  └─ Yes: continue
│
├─ Is there a raw record?
│  ├─ No: collect what's missing; wait for a new raw record
│  └─ Yes: continue
│
├─ Is the current revision recorded?
│  ├─ No: mark the version as unknown; don't merge it into an older object with the same name
│  └─ Yes: find the most recent normal record
│
└─ Can you view the normal record alongside the captured state?
   ├─ No: preserve the captured state; stop here: comparison missing
   └─ Yes: look only for the first difference
```

The "most recent normal record" isn't just any green result. It should come from the same type of entry point, without intermediate information being collapsed into just the final status. If the green record is much later than the anomaly, or has been reclassified, it can only be listed as a lead, not used in place of the original comparison record.

Follow one direction at a time when comparing. First ask whether the raw record entered the Quality Signal Console, then which step inside the console it stopped at. If the first difference is at the entry point or in the environment, stop on the entry-point side first; only continue into internal processing if the first difference is inside the console. If the first difference requires external permissions or interface clarification, don't name a root cause on the other party's behalf when handing it off.

## From the difference to the handoff point

```text
First difference between the raw record and the normal record
├─ Difference is at the current entry point
│  ├─ Screenshot has a source: return to the entry point and account that produced it
│  └─ Screenshot has no source: mark as supporting evidence; wait for a traceable record
├─ Difference is inside the Quality Signal Console
│  ├─ Input still exists: preserve the input and first output; continue within the project
│  └─ Input has been cleared out: stop at the missing record; don't rerun to fill in the story
├─ Difference is only in the environment
│  ├─ Conditions can be documented: preserve the conditions, then make one more comparison
│  └─ Conditions can't be described clearly: don't treat the retry result as recovery
└─ Difference crosses an interface boundary
   ├─ Permissions needed: hand off to the permissions owner with the supporting material
   └─ Interface change needed: pause this runbook; follow the formal review process separately
```

The scope for continuing within the project is narrow: it only covers the Quality Signal Console's own inputs, regression tiering, flaky-signal attribution, or gaps in the records directly caused by those objects. Anything requiring external accounts, external interfaces, or changes to the user-visible contract is outside the scope of continuing under this page. When handing off, include the current entry point, current revision, raw record location, first difference, and known environment differences.

The permissions owner may confirm that the permissions side is unrelated, or may send the issue back. A return doesn't mean the Quality Signal Console should immediately start a second round of guessing: first attach the reasons for the return alongside the original record, then continue from the first difference that still holds. If the returned material doesn't say which observation was invalidated, stop due to insufficient handoff information.

## Two wrong turns to watch for

**Treating green as recovery.** The early records include one case where a retry was run before the first failing sample was saved, leaving only a green result. At most, that shows that one later execution did not remain stalled; it doesn't show recovery under the original conditions. The order now is to save the first failing sample and environment differences before deciding whether to retry; put the retry output after the original sample.

**Inferring intermediate steps from the final display.** Directory names, summary numbers, and the final page may all have gone through classification. They can help locate the entry point, but cannot prove which steps the raw record went through. If only the final display is available, record "display visible, original process unknown" and stop there.

## Assessment after conditions are locked down

When working with older material, record these cases separately: if an old record doesn't include the current revision, keep it marked as version unknown; if it has a version but lacks environment details, you can compare the contents but cannot rule out environmental factors; place new raw records captured after conditions were locked down alongside the old samples; if it hasn't been seen again after conditions were locked down, write only "not seen again".

Release classification is only one layer of context. If the anomaly was first discovered after classification, first confirm whether the record for that occurrence at the current entry point can be traced; if it can't, retain "discovered after classification, source not recovered". Don't write down classification as the cause just because the timing is close.

CACHEB-002 is for linking back to the missing original evidence, and CACHEB-003 is for tracing screenshot sources. Both cards are navigation points; later statuses on the cards cannot replace the first sample saved here. The handoff entry point is still `docs/adj-query-codemods/runbooks/query-codemods-quality-signal-blocked-escalation-contacts.md`.
