If all you can obtain is a screenshot, first note which entry point and account it came from. If the source cannot be obtained, the screenshot can still be retained, but label it "supporting evidence" alongside it; it must not be used to directly conclude that a particular input has entered the Quality Signal Console. If neither a screenshot nor an original record exists, record only where the anomaly was seen and the known points in time, then wait for a new capture. At this stage, do not discuss the root cause or attach a common issue label.

The current revision is another independent piece of information. When it is missing, same-named objects must not be automatically merged; write "version unknown" in the record. Even if the version is found later, it should be appended after the original record, rather than backfilled as though it had been known from the start. This lets reviewers distinguish assessments made at the time from material added later.

## Follow this tree first

```text
Quality Signal Console is stuck
│
├─ Can the current entry point be located?
│  ├─ No
│  │  └─ Retain the existing description and screenshots; mark the entry point as missing; stop
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ Is there an original record?
│     │  ├─ No
│     │  │  └─ Track down the entry point and account; do not name a root cause before collecting additional data
│     │  └─ Yes
│     │     ├─ Is the current revision known?
│     │     │  ├─ No: keep the version marked as unknown, do not merge records when looking for similar ones
│     │     │  └─ Yes: continue
│     │     └─ Is there a readable normal record?
│     │        ├─ No: stop at the missing comparison record
│     │        └─ Yes: find the first difference
│     └─ Is only a cleaned-up version of the screenshot available?
│        └─ It can only help locate the source, not replace the original record
```

Every stopping point in this tree is a useful outcome. Stopping does not mean giving up; it means the available materials are insufficient to proceed safely to the next branch. Writing "entry point missing," "original records missing," "version unknown," or "comparison missing" at the actual point of blockage makes it easier for the person taking over to supply the right materials than a blanket "still to be confirmed."

A minimal record can contain just four lines: the current entry point, whether original records exist, whether the current revision is known, and which item is blocking the next step. For more complex incidents, also attach the environment differences, screenshot sources, and what was first seen. Do not rewrite logs just to fill out a form; an appendix containing the material as-is is more valuable than a cleaned-up retelling.

## A normal record is not just any green result

Some workflows rerun immediately after the first failure and then show green. That green result only indicates that the later execution did not remain blocked; it does not prove recovery from the initial failure. Earlier practice treated retries as the default recovery action, which caused both the first failure sample and the environment differences to be lost; subsequent investigations could only work backward from the final display, directory names, or memory, with no way to confirm where the differences began.

The sequence is now fixed:

1. Preserve the first failure sample.
2. Write down the environment differences visible at the time.
3. Find a normal record of the same type.
4. Compare only the earliest difference.
5. Then decide whether to retry.

A "normal record of the same type" must at least come from a comparable entry point and must not be a processed result with only the final display remaining. If the normal record has been reclassified, lacks a version, or is too far removed in time from the incident, it can only serve as a lead. A lead can help identify the next step, but cannot justify closing this incident.

When comparing, do not change the entry point, sample, and environment at the same time. Follow only one difference at a time: first check whether the original records reached the Quality Signal Dashboard, then whether they are still visible within it, and then whether the environment differs. If multiple conditions are changed at once, even if subsequent results turn green, there is no way to know which condition changed the outcome.

## The first difference determines which way to go

```text
Where does the first difference appear?
├─ Current entry point
│  ├─ Screenshots or records with known sources
│  │  └─ Return to that entry point to verify the account and original materials
│  └─ Only unsourced screenshots
│     └─ Label as supporting evidence; stop at missing source
├─ Inside the Quality Signal Dashboard
│  ├─ The original input is still present
│  │  └─ Stay within the project and continue examining classification or unstable signals
│  └─ Only processed results remain from the input
│     └─ Stop at missing records, do not use a rerun to backfill the old process
├─ Environment
│  ├─ Conditions can be documented clearly
│  │  └─ A single comparison is allowed after saving the conditions
│  └─ Conditions cannot be documented clearly
│     └─ Preserve the difference; do not describe the new result as recovery from the original failure
└─ Clearly outside the interface
   ├─ Permissions need to be obtained
   │  └─ Hand off to the permissions owner with the materials
   └─ The shared interface needs to change
      └─ Stop using this page, switch to formal review
```

The first difference is not the easiest one to explain. The final page differs from the normal page, but that does not mean the difference must be inside the quality signal dashboard; first confirm where the original record corresponding to the page is. Seeing a different directory name or summary number also does not mean that intermediate processing has taken place, because these items may come from later categorization. They can only lead someone back to the entry point and should not be treated as process evidence.

If the original record shows that the difference is at the current entry, do not continue guessing inside the quality signal dashboard about what happened after the input. First find the account and entry that produced the record, then confirm whether the screenshot was produced at the same location. If the account cannot be found, record this gap and stop. Do not fill in a nonexistent source with "someone has seen a similar problem before."

If the difference is inside the quality signal dashboard, retain the input, current revision, and first visible output. Within the project, you can continue checking regression stratification and unstable-signal attribution; but once the next step requires reading the status of an external project, asking someone else to change an interface, or explaining behavior seen by external users, do not continue along the internal path. At that point, hand over the known materials rather than writing external objects into the internal conclusion.

If the difference is limited to an environmental difference, first document the conditions that can be stated clearly. When the environmental conditions cannot be clearly described, it is acceptable to retain the observation "an environment difference exists," but do not claim that it is the cause. A new comparison can be run once the conditions have been recorded; the comparison result should be stored alongside the old incident evidence. When the new comparison does not get stuck again, write "not seen again in the new sample"; do not rewrite the status of the old record.

## Keep the old conditions even after the toolchain is fixed

Once the toolchain is fixed, a common misunderstanding is to assume that the old evidence is no longer valid. Fixing the toolchain only constrains conditions for collection going forward. It cannot retroactively fill in records that were missing in the past. When handling old materials, distinguish them as follows:

| Observed combination | How to record it | What can be determined |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The old record has no current revision | Mark the version as unknown | Do not merge it directly with an object of the same name |
| The old record has a version but no environment | Preserve the version and the missing environment | Content can be compared; do not rule out the environment |
| After the toolchain is fixed, there is a new original record | Keep it alongside the old sample | The first difference between the new and old samples can be identified |
| The issue does not appear again after the toolchain is fixed | Record it as not seen again in the new sample | Cannot record it as recovered |
| Only a green result after a retry remains | Place it after the first sample | Cannot replace the first sample |

Fixing the toolchain mainly prevents subsequent collection from changing the conditions each time. It does not provide evidence that an error has disappeared, nor does it determine who it should be handed to. Handoff is still determined by the first difference and the interface boundary.

The same applies when a release has already been categorized. Categorization indicates that someone placed the relevant records in a release context; it does not indicate that the release caused the process to get stuck. If the anomaly was first seen after categorization, first check whether that item's current entry can be traced back to the original record. If it cannot be traced, write "found after categorization; source not recovered." Do not directly record the categorization as the cause merely because the times are close.

The status indicating that handling has started also cannot replace the incident evidence. It only means someone has taken over to inspect it. If the original incident materials are still missing, stop at the missing-material branch; if the original materials are already available, continue looking for the first difference. Do not treat "started" as "reproduced" or "handed off."

## Scope for continuing within the project

The quality signal dashboard can continue handling samples whose formation failed within it, regression stratification, unstable-signal attribution, and record gaps that directly block these tasks. Continuing here does not mean expanding the investigation indefinitely: each time, answer only the one question required by the current branch.

For example, if the original input is still available but quality signals have stopped appearing, you can retain the input, compare it with a normal sample to find the first difference, and then check whether that difference falls within this project's own classification scope. If the difference is still on the current entry-point side, return to the entry point; if external permissions are required to see the next record, hand it off; if continuing requires changing a shared interface, stop following this page.

Do not keep trying to force an investigation within the project when it involves the following:

- Needing another project to grant permissions to obtain the original record;
- Needing to explain behavior seen by external users or callers;
- Needing to change a shared interface;
- Needing to use internal state from elsewhere to prove a hypothesis on this page;
- Needing to merge multiple old objects with the same name without version information.

These situations do not mean that the Quality Signal Desk has left its work unfinished. What it has done is bring the observed situation to the boundary and identify which gap prevents further assessment.

## Materials to hand off to the permissions owner

A handoff is not just "please take a look". Before handing it off to the permissions owner, put together the following minimal package:

```text
Current entry point: ……
Current revision: known / unknown
Original record: location or explanation of what is missing
What was first observed: ……
Normal record: location or indication that a comparison record is missing
First difference: ……
Environment differences: known / unknown
Required permissions: ……
```

"What was first observed" should stay as close as possible to the original record, rather than being condensed into a label such as "abnormal signal". "First difference" should likewise describe only the point actually reached in the comparison, without extending it into a judgment about the cause. If the permissions owner confirms that there are no relevant materials on the permissions side, attach that response alongside the original record; then continue from a branch that still holds, rather than treating unanswered parts as already ruled out.

If you discover after the handoff that the screenshot's source was recorded incorrectly, correct the source directly alongside the screenshot and retain the previous annotation. Do not delete the old annotation without a trace, or later readers will mistakenly think the source was certain from the start. If you discover that the current revision was previously recorded incorrectly, likewise append a correction and separate the same-named objects again; do not use the new version to overwrite the provenance of the old assessment.

## A shared interface is an explicit stopping point

When the next step requires changing a shared interface, stop following this page. The on-call log can explain why work stopped here: the existing original records already show that the difference crosses the Quality Signal Desk's boundary, or continuing requires changing an externally visible contract. It does not replace a formal review to select a solution.

If someone wants to bypass the interface issue by retrying, reclassifying, or switching to another entry point, first return to the original situation. New results produced after the bypass can serve as new samples, but they do not eliminate the need to hand off the original situation. A "success" that does not retain the original input and the first difference cannot explain why the original record got stuck.

## Separate handling for screenshots and broken links

Screenshots can easily lose their connection to the entry point as they are passed around. Handle them in the following order:

```text
A screenshot appears
├─ The entry point and account that produced it can be found
│  ├─ The original record can be found: use the screenshot as supplementary material
│  └─ The original record cannot be found: record that the entry point is known and the original record is missing
└─ The entry point or account that produced it cannot be found
   ├─ A comparable normal record is still available: use it only to suggest a direction for further investigation
   └─ None is available: mark as circumstantial evidence, stop
```

Do not treat it as an independent reproduction just because a second colleague can see the same screenshot. The second person can only retrace the steps using the existing materials; if an entry point, account, version, or original record is missing at any step, document the gap beside that step. The incident evidence preserved with these breaks in the chain is still useful: it tells those who come later which part is missing not because it never happened, but because it was not brought back.

When quality signal objects with the same name lack version identifiers, treat this as a broken chain as well. Do not stitch together a continuous history based on similar names. Keep the objects separate first, and wait for the current revision or original records to be supplied; until then, any claim that an object is "already the same as the old object" can only be considered speculation.

## Boundaries for retries

Retries are not prohibited, but they must come after preserving the incident evidence. If you retry:

1. First confirm that the first failed sample has been preserved unchanged;
2. Record the current entry point, current revision, and known environment;
3. Change only one explicitly documented condition;
4. Append the retry output as a new sample;
5. Do not overwrite the failed sample with green output;
6. If the new sample is still stuck, continue investigating from the first difference between the two records;
7. If the new sample is normal, state that it coexists with the old sample, and keep the gaps in the old incident evidence documented.

If the first failed sample was not saved, do not try to "recover" it through repeated retries. Every output obtained later describes only a later execution. At this point, the most valuable action is to track down the entry point, account, screenshot source, and any original materials that may still be available, rather than generate more green results that cannot be compared.

## Where to stop during an on-call shift

In the following cases, work can be paused temporarily within the quality signal console:

| Incident state | How to pause |
| --- | --- |
| The original records, version, and first difference are all available, and the difference is still within the project | Continue handling it within the project |
| Original records are missing | Note the location of the gap, and wait for the missing records to be collected |
| The screenshot has no source | Label it as supporting evidence, and wait for an entry point or account |
| Normal-run records are not comparable | Stop at the missing comparison, without working backward from the final display |
| Environments differ, but not all conditions are known | Preserve the environmental differences, without naming a cause |
| The next step requires external permissions | Attach a minimal package of materials and hand off to the permissions owner |
| The next step requires a shared interface change | Stop work on this page, and move to formal review |

When pausing, do not record "no new results yet" as "no issues". Likewise, even if green output arrives later, do not change the incident state to "recovered". The value of on-call records lies in preserving the branches as they stood at the time, not in making every entry look finished in the end.

## Card entry point

CACHEB-002 is used to link back to issues involving missing information from the original incident. When handling this card, prioritize supplying the current entry point, current revision, and what was first seen; if only a screenshot can be supplied, it should still be labeled as supporting evidence.

CACHEB-003 is used to trace the source of the screenshot for the current entry point. First find the entry point and account that produced the screenshot. If they cannot be found, leave the source marked as missing on the card; do not replace it with a green sample curated later.

CACHEB-002 and CACHEB-003 are only responsible for directing people to the relevant materials. Any status change, toolchain pinning, release categorization, or start of processing on the card must return to the specific branch decision: did they fill in the original record, the normal control, and the first divergence? If they did not, continue to retain the corresponding stop point.

## Fallback After Handoff

The person taking over may give one of three responses: find materials on the permissions side, confirm that no materials exist on the permissions side, or point out that a key item is missing from the handoff package. For the first type, attach the new material after the original record, then reassess the first divergence; for the second type, attach the "not found on the permissions side" response back, without expanding it into other paths having been ruled out; for the third type, prioritize filling the missing item, and do not continue reasoning from the gap.

If, after handoff, it turns out that the divergence is still within the quality signal dashboard's own scope, simply return to the project with the basis for returning it and continue. Do not let an external project stand in for this page in preserving the evidence just because the issue has already been handed off once. Conversely, if an in-project check finds that an external interface is needed, stop checking and route it to formal review; do not quietly hard-code the interface choice in the handoff record.

When you need to return to this page, start from the last branch that still has original material, not from the previous conclusion summarized from memory. If the record has already been curated, prioritize recovering the first sample; if it cannot be recovered, explicitly stop at missing material.

## Old Judgments Still Retained

Old records once treated "turning green after a retry" as a signal of on-site recovery. This judgment no longer applies, but the related records are still retained because they explain why some early entries contain only the final result and no first failure sample. Another old habit was to check the release side first whenever a release categorization appeared; now treat the categorization only as temporal context, and first confirm whether the original record for the anomaly can be retrieved.

These corrections do not require cleaning the old materials into a uniform format. When reviewing early entries, it should still be clear which material was missing at the time. Place information recovered later after the old record, and label whether it fills in the entry point, version, control, or permissions-side response.

Apart from CACHEB-002 and CACHEB-003, DOC-36 retains an earlier intermediate record. It only goes as far as `pending promise` and `framework adaptation`; it has no direct caller. That record is suitable for explaining the breakpoint, but is not sufficient to replace the original sample on this page. When reading it, still keep the current entry point, version, and first divergence separate.

One final check: if the next step can only rely on guessing the account, caller, permissions, or interface, stop at the current node; if the next step can obtain a new divergence from a saved original record, continue only along that one.

# Documentation Site Window Closeout Checklist

This checklist is a working page left over from an early window, and its scope is still narrow: borrowing at the current entry point, the final output, the return time, and the backout entry point for adj-react-query. It does not list every publishing step for the documentation site or check docs, guide, and release notes item by item. Content borrowed temporarily during a window can easily lose its context when the window ends, so start by putting the borrowed item, times, and output in one place.

## Record the details when opening the window

- [ ] Next to `docs/adj-react-query/release/react-query-documentation-portal-pre-window-close-checklist.md`, specify what is being borrowed this time, not just "documentation site" or "current entry point."
- [ ] Record the start time and return deadline. No borrowing can enter the window without specified times; if the times have not been decided, leave it pending confirmation rather than treating it as logged.
- [ ] Save the output visible before starting. It does not have to be a complete report, but you must be able to put it alongside the final output from before closeout; do not leave only "success."
- [ ] If the window reuses a regression matrix from an old page, record its name as well. The old version only said "find the regression matrix"; the matrix is no substitute for the borrowed item and return time.

## Keep only two comparable snapshots during the borrowing period

Borrowed content can continue to be used at the current entry point, but the fact that the page still opens does not mean the borrowing can be extended automatically. Each time you are about to continue, first check the return deadline in the record, then save a copy of the output at that moment. "Final output" here means the last result seen before the window closes, not a success screenshot prepared after the return.

If the entry point's content changes, you cannot keep relying only on the initial output. Put the initial output alongside the post-change output, and note whether the entry-point material was replaced in between. There is no need to backfill every check, but it must at least be clear which borrowing the final output corresponds to; otherwise, do not combine the two sets of results into one when closing the window.

The old version also said, "Do not clear the state after seeing attribute tracing." This sentence remains because it was indeed used as a reminder during the window at the time; it does not, by itself, mean the window can be closed. When attribute tracing appears, preserve the state first, then still verify the borrowed content, return time, and final output. Not seeing it is no reason to delete output that has already been saved, either.

The documentation site's docs, guide, and release notes each have their own maintenance cadence. This checklist does not decide whether their content is out of date, nor does it use release notes to decide whether to back out. Closeout here only concerns whether the borrowed content can be returned on time and whether the final output has been retained. If temporary diagnostics change the entry point, first mark that output as not directly comparable, then decide whether to keep the window open.

## Action order before closing the window

1. **Verify the borrowed content.** Check against the item recorded when the window opened and confirm that the current entry point still has the same content. If it has been replaced with something else, do not close the window using the old record as-is; stop further operations and retain the old and new items separately.
2. **Save the final output.** Save the last visible result before the return and keep it alongside the initial output. If there is only a "success" label with no actual content, still treat it as having no saved sample; do not wait until after the return to add a screenshot.
3. **Verify the return time.** Complete the return before the deadline. If the time is unclear, the borrower is unknown, or the return action has not been confirmed, leave the window in an unconfirmed state rather than assuming it "should already have been returned."
4. **Use the backout entry point.** If the borrowed content cannot be returned, the final output is missing, or the entry point is no longer the one in the record, exit through the backout entry point for adj-react-query. Do not continue borrowing while waiting for additional evidence, and do not clear the state first.

When `signal injection` did not appear, the old checklist required stopping here. This stopping point is still retained, but it only describes how things were done at the time and does not override the four checks above; even if the text appears, borrowing and output must still be confirmed individually. If you stop here, mark the window as incomplete and retain what has already been saved.

## Two closeout failure modes

**The final output is present, but the return is not yet confirmed.** Do not close the window. Output is only a record; it does not mean the borrowing has ended. Preserve the current state and proceed through the backout entry point; do not clean up early just to show completion.

**The return is complete, but the final output was not saved.** Do not mark this as a normal closeout either. Do not rerun after the return and pass off the new result as output from before the window closed. Explicitly record the missing output as missing; if the work must be redone, open another window rather than inserting the new window's results into this record.

If the state already resembles a failed run recorded in DOC-38, preserve the final output first, then handle the backout. If recovery actions cannot be confirmed in the shared environment, do not document untried recovery actions as executable steps; that gap from the old version remains on this page.

## For the next person who opens a window

At the end of this window, it should be possible to find at least the borrowed content, start time, return deadline, initial output, final output, and whether the backout entry point was used. If any one is missing, keep the status incomplete. This checklist does not decide the documentation site's long-term maintenance approach, nor does it treat entry-point reachability as proof of return.

The old version placed more weight on "find the regression matrix" and entry-point reachability than on return records; this version puts the borrowed item, times, and saved samples ahead of the closeout actions, while retaining the old reminders and traces of how they were used. The checklist only records window closeout; unfinished recovery actions remain in TODO.

# Documentation Site Cache: Setup Trade-offs and Decision

We decided to keep `current revision` and not rebuild the react-query-documentation-portal environment. Rebuilding would mix environment changes into the comparison, so the original setup and the new results could no longer be assessed under the same conditions. First preserve the existing pages, inputs, and failure exits already observed, then discuss the implementation trade-offs.

At the time, we were comparing two approaches: continue handling page state through the `query observer`, or split out `online status`. The first approach looked like it would require fewer changes, but it placed different failure exits at the same observation point. Once the pages showed differences, it was hard to tell whether the query results had changed or online status itself had changed. The second approach required reconfirming the callers in use, especially since the list of places using `region notifications` was still incomplete; its cost was clearer, but page behavior and state changes could be reviewed separately.

We chose the separation approach and made preserving the setup a condition for this round of comparison. `current revision` is not a permanently fixed baseline, nor does it require all subsequent work to stay on the old pages; it only preserves the pages, inputs, and failure exits on which this trade-off was based. If the implementation or page content changes, keep a separate comparison record. Green results in a new environment must not be retroactively recorded as evidence that this choice was already justified.

The argument for retaining the `query observer` was not without merit. Existing pages may still get their values from it. Separation would increase the integration surface and could scatter state that was previously viewed in one place across two locations. The reason we did not choose this approach was that the two failure exits in this record need to be explained separately—not that the `query observer` can no longer be used. Pages that need to continue using the old entry point can remain unchanged until the actual caller relationships are fully mapped.

Another objection concerned `region notifications`. It was already present on the page side, but its active callers had not been confirmed; this is not grounds to assume that splitting out `online status` has covered all pages, nor can unconfirmed integration points be counted as migrated. The decision is therefore narrow in scope: preserve the original setup, pursue separation, and do not yet include callers that have not been found in the conclusion.

We also do not assume that the exit procedure is "just restore the old entry point." If `current revision` needs to be released later, first save the pages and inputs used at that time and the last identifiable failure exit, then assess whether restoring the old entry point is enough. Otherwise, the environment switch itself would erase the comparison conditions, leaving no way to tell whether differences came from implementation changes or from the rebuilt setup.

Start the review at `docs/adj-react-query/decisions/react-query-documentation-portal-cache-vs-original-context-tradeoffs.md`. That location retains this choice and the two objections. If caller relationships for `region notifications` are filled in later, or the results after exit are confirmed, they should be appended as a new decision record, without rewriting the context for this trade-off.

## Inputs for the Next Decision

Reopen this trade-off only after obtaining the actual caller relationships for `region notifications`, results from the original pages under the same conditions, and a comparison after exit. Label each of the three artifacts with its collection time and reviewer; if any one is missing, keep the existing decision and do not override the original setup with a single green result from a new environment.

# Package Integration Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

The same vue query integration record reported different current revisions at two points in time. On the first check, property tracking differed from the old record; the original record was still there, but the recovery page showed a different result. The initial impact was on review and exit decisions: at one point, all that could be confirmed was that "two states had been observed." That was not enough to determine which state represented the final result, and retries could not continue based solely on the last line of green output.

## Changes During the Incident

- The initial record captured the discrepancy, not its cause. It only noted that property tracking was inconsistent with the old record; it did not present the change in the retryer as the cause. Missing points in the timeline were not filled in with guesses, and the original record and recovery page were saved separately.
- The subsequent on-call handoff added versions, request context, and stop conditions. The review started from `docs/adj-vue-query/incidents/vue-query-package-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`, first preserving the version combination seen at the time, then checking whether the two records still pointed to the same object.
- On the next check, signal injection could restore the environment. This showed only that the recovery path worked, not why the two states had appeared; the record still had no answer for why the retryer changed.

## Timeline and Impact

The first sign of the anomaly was property tracking results diverging from the old record. The recovery page then showed another result. The two pages each captured a different point in time, leaving reviewers unable to tell from a single page whether version synchronization was complete. After the on-call handoff, request context, versions, and stop conditions began to be saved together. This reduced repeated trial and error but did not fill in the missing intermediate points in time.

The scope of impact was recorded at the time in terms of cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer integration. It affected the review order and exit decisions. The available material did not establish that adjacent services had already been affected in the same way, and speculation about adjacent services was not included as a cause. The project still had its own schedule, maintainer, and exit conditions; the two states could not be merged into a single maintenance target just because they appeared in the same record.

## Response and Outstanding Issues

If the two states reappear, first stop retrying, save the entry page, exit code, and last log segment, then check them against the existing regression matrix. Signal injection can be recorded as a recovery action that has already been tried; after recovery, do not delete the original record or infer the cause of the failure from successful recovery. A later addendum separated the impact window from the recovery action and preserved what remained unconfirmed at the time.

This page retains the assessment from the earlier point in time: the property tracking discrepancy was the first clue to surface, and signal injection was a recovery action that had already been tried. The available record has not confirmed a direct connection between the two; the cause of the retryer change also remains unresolved. Continue handling subsequent branches through the project's maintenance pages. Do not overwrite the original record, recovery page, or unconfirmed causes with a single new result.

title: Proposal for an Alternative Package Integration Approach

versions.body:
# Alternative Package Integration Approach

The package integration work originally kept two options open: continue with "pause changes," or separate the error boundary from the existing integration. This record covers only the second approach, which never reached a trial, and why it was not accepted at the time.

The biggest benefit of "pause changes" was leaving the entry point unchanged. Callers would still get results through the existing composition, and investigation would only require looking at one exit. The problem was that the two failure exits identified in the material represented different situations: one stops during integration, while the other only becomes an error after the combined result has been formed. Collapsing both into a paused state makes the recovery actions look the same, while leaving it unclear which point to return to.

The idea behind separating out the error boundary was to give integration failures and combined-result failures their own exits. This would not replace the existing package flow; it would only move follow-up observation to a point where the two types of failure could be distinguished. The objection was straightforward: once the boundary was independent, callers would need to know which part of the result they had received, but it was not yet clear which callers were using the "combined result" at the time.

The split was therefore not made the default approach. Keeping it as an option required confirming that at least one caller could still handle the original combined result outside the boundary; otherwise, the new exit would only move the existing uncertainty elsewhere. No start time was set and no one had taken on the trial, so this cannot be treated as having taken effect.

The rollback criteria were written more briefly than the trial steps: if integration errors and combined-result errors cannot be distinguished after the split, or if callers can only get results through the old entry point, restore the original entry point rather than continuing to patch in compatibility layers locally. Here, "restore" refers only to that entry point; it does not mean other exit actions have been completed.

Another open item is the pending promise. It is tied to whether the error boundary is separated out, but there is not enough material yet to determine whether it belongs on the integration side or the result side. Do not choose an approach based on it yet; decide whether to reopen the discussion once the scope of callers can be checked.

The supporting material is still at `docs/adj-vue-query/proposals/unused-vue-query-package-integration-approach.md`. Records of similar approaches may use the same "pause changes" wording, but they should not be used to fill in caller relationships that were not confirmed here.

## Material Needed to Reopen the Discussion

If the split approach is raised again, first have a caller still using the old entry point provide records of an integration failure and a combined-result failure for the same input, then designate someone responsible for rollback. If the two types of results cannot be pinpointed separately, keep the proposal on hold; treat the pending promise only as an open item, not as grounds for a conclusion about caller scope. The record must also retain the trial start time, observation window, and results after restoring the old entry point.

It does not mean withdrawal is complete or that legacy callers have passed regression testing. This page still cannot confirm whether adapter invocation samples are covered.

After finding the entry point, you can return to the maintenance records to investigate the candidate path, but do not mark the path as withdrawn. Even if a legacy caller is passing regression testing at that point, that only establishes the result of that regression run; it cannot replace confirmation of who owns the candidate path, much less confirmation of the final cache state. DOC-50 document single-variable reruns for the cross-framework window. Do not use them to fill the gap in adapter samples here.

## Who is responsible for withdrawing candidate paths?

Withdrawal of a candidate path must be confirmed by the corresponding maintenance owner. The person who viewed the entry point, the person who performed the review, and the implementer have distinct responsibilities. The implementer can add review results to the record, but cannot close a candidate item just because they ran it once. If the corresponding owner has not yet been found, keep the target pending confirmation in the record. Do not count withdrawal as complete because the path appears at the type-contract entry point or because a caller is temporarily passing.

Two mix-ups are common here: treating the person who most recently modified the file as the path owner, or treating the person whose reply is pending as someone who has already confirmed. This page does not have enough evidence to support either. If the owner list was not retained in full, keeping the targets and blank entries is more accurate than filling in a seemingly certain name.

## Under what conditions can the card be closed?

A release card can be closed out only when all three conditions are met at the same time: each accumulated node has been rerun, regression tests for legacy callers remain green, and someone other than the implementer has confirmed the final cache state. Here, "at the same time" does not mean writing the results in a single record; it means all three are accounted for in the maintenance records. If even one is missing, the card cannot be marked complete.

Unrun combinations and callers that have not replied must continue to be left explicitly blank; "there are no new failures at present" cannot stand in for them. If the accumulated nodes have been rerun but there are still no regression results for legacy callers, the card remains incomplete. If regression tests are green but no one other than the implementer has confirmed the final cache state, the card still cannot be closed out. Entry-point visibility cannot fill the gap in adapter invocation samples either.

### Earlier wording retained for reference

The early version blurred the distinctions between the entry point, path status, and closure. The later review did not carry that equivalence forward. It only revised the scope of what could be confirmed and retained this old question for reference. The corresponding targets for the adapter invocation samples are still missing, and there is no complete list of candidate-path owners. The records support "being able to look it up does not mean it has been withdrawn"; that statement cannot be used to infer that withdrawal is complete.

This page retains only the judgments directly related to the three questions: where to start looking, who can confirm withdrawal, and which results must all be present before closure. Leave unanswered parts blank. Do not use adjacent records or a single regression run that passed at the time to answer them.

This round compared two approaches before the freeze date: continue using the current mutation-runtime entry point, or adjust the processing window during the rotation. The decision is to retain the current entry point at this stage; adjusting the window is only a candidate and will not replace the existing path before the freeze.

Any unresolved item left before the freeze date must specify an owner, a reproduction entry point, and rollback conditions. If any one of these is missing, it does not count as an item that can be handed over with the rotation.

versions.body:
# On-Call Rotation Release Freeze Decision Record

This discussion began with a seemingly simple handoff problem: with the release freeze approaching, the on-call rotation cannot change the handling entry point, expand coverage, and hand an issue that has not yet been reproduced to the next on-call teammate at the same time. The initial draft focused on "whether the window should be adjusted"; review confirmed that what actually needs to be fixed first is who, during handoff, can determine whether an unresolved item can be retained, withdrawn, or must be stopped before the freeze.

The meeting compared two paths.

The first is to retain the current mutation-runtime entry point. It does not require the rotating personnel to familiarize themselves with another set of entry points before the freeze, nor does it change how existing callers observe results to a new standard. The cost is that the window adjustment cannot be rolled out with this release; the parts requiring adjustment still need to separately document their observed results, counterexamples, and withdrawal actions.

The second is to adjust the window and have the on-call rotation handle work according to the new path. The benefit of this option is that it brings the subsequent arrangements forward into this round, but the materials that could be confirmed at the time covered only part of the behavior. When the entry point, the results seen by caller Fang Ke, and the same-entry counterexamples have not all been collected within the same scope, the window itself is not suitable as a replacement path before the freeze, even if it appears usable.

Decision: continue using the current mutation-runtime entry point during the freeze. Keep the window adjustment as a later candidate; do not replace the existing entry point with it in this release. This decision does not permanently reject the adjustment proposal; it downgrades it from "a change that can be handed off this round" back to "a candidate requiring its judgment conditions to be completed."

## Freeze Boundary

Unresolved items that arise before the freeze date must include all three of the following:

- a current owner who can state who will continue deciding the item, rather than merely being the person who logged it;
- a publicly accessible reproduction entry point that lets the person taking over return to the same observation point;
- withdrawal conditions that clearly state what result triggers withdrawal of the candidate path or stopping further progress.

If any one of the three is missing, the status on the page should remain migrating or pending confirmation. It must not be rewritten as completed just because the on-call rotation is about to change. Here, owner means the entry point for technical decisions; it does not automatically make the person who recorded the live situation the implementation sign-off owner. The person who logged it is responsible for preserving the live context; only the corresponding module owner, QA, or interface maintainer may complete the technical review.

A "reproduction entry point" cannot be just a vague module name. The handoff requires an entry point that the person taking over can open, along with the minimum observation conditions: which caller to enter from, what result to see, and what result would constitute a same-entry counterexample. The purpose is not to establish an additional approval process, but to prevent someone after the rotation from having to guess the original phenomenon from the old description.

The withdrawal conditions must also apply to the candidate path itself. If adjusting the window makes it impossible to maintain the observable result for a known caller, or if a counterexample shows that the new and old entry points produce different behavior under the same conditions, withdraw that candidate path and continue using the current entry point. Withdrawal does not mean that the issue has disappeared; it simply separates the path that can be safely continued during on-call duty from the path that requires separate validation.

## Judgments Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial draft presented "adjust the window" as a handoff choice parallel to "retain the entry point" and assumed that, as long as the rotation schedule was clear, the window could be switched first. This judgment was not deleted because it explains why the handoff conditions were later added: the rotation schedule only resolves who takes over, not what the person taking over uses to determine that the behavior remains within the original scope.

The original intent in the initial draft was:

> If adjusting the window can reduce duplicate handling during handoff, it can be enabled before the freeze, and the next shift can complete caller confirmation.

This guidance no longer applies. It places caller confirmation after the path switch, which means that if a counterexample appears during the freeze, on-call personnel must both restore the old path and find the original entry point. After review, this was changed to first confirm the scope covered by existing evidence; uncovered parts do not move with the release.

The old draft also had an overly permissive statement: an unresolved item could be handed off as long as it had a person responsible for it. The later requirements make clear that, in addition to a responsible person, a reproduction entry point and withdrawal conditions are required. This old wording is retained to prevent later readers from mistakenly assuming that "all three items are present" was always the original rule.

## Division of Responsibilities After Review

Technical review was not divided evenly by participant count this round. The roles able to review depend on which object the issue concerns: the corresponding module owner can confirm the entry point and behavior scope; QA can confirm whether the minimum reproduction still holds; the interface maintainer can confirm whether the caller can still see the same result. If any one of the three raises a same-entry counterexample, the candidate path must not proceed merely because it is marked "registered."

The on-call personnel's role is narrower. They maintain the status during the freeze, preserve the live context, and hand off items that have all three pieces of information; when a record has no owner, no reproduction entry point, or no withdrawal conditions, they should stop where it is and fill in the missing pieces. On-call personnel do not judge the module implementation because of the rotation, nor do they confirm cross-package behavior on behalf of people who did not participate in the review.

This boundary tightens the previous way of working. Previously, someone treated "someone is already looking at it" as grounds to let it through. After review, two things were distinguished: someone paying attention to an issue, and someone able to make a withdrawal judgment on the candidate path during the freeze, are not the same thing. The former can remain in the status record; the latter constitutes a handoff condition.

## Material Placement

During the release period, cards retain only status changes and the next step; they do not carry the complete technical rationale. Stable decisions, the approved scope, and the reasons for rejected options are placed in reviewed documentation. This allows later readers to find why the entry point was retained at the time and why the window adjustment did not enter with this release.

Chat retains the reproductions, waiting, corrections, and referrals from the time. A local observation appearing in chat cannot automatically be elevated to a release decision, especially not expanded from a single description while waiting to all cross-package behavior. If a new observation changes the assessment of the candidate path, first add the entry point, counterexample, or withdrawal condition required by this decision, and then update the status record.

This separation is not intended to scatter the same chain of causality across different places. The card tells on-call where the work stopped; chat preserves why it stopped at the time; this record preserves the choice that was made and its applicable scope. Each retains only the portion useful for handoff.

## Scope Approved This Round

The scope approved this round is limited to cross-package behavior that existing evidence can cover. The criterion is not whether the internal implementations appear similar, but whether the caller can observe the result and whether a same-entry counterexample has been checked. For objects that meet this criterion, the current entry point can continue to be used through the on-call rotation.

Uncovered objects are not automatically included because their names are similar, their entry points are adjacent, or a window adjustment is planned. Putting them into the same freeze decision would make the meaning of "retain the current entry point" unclear: some people would interpret it as confirmed compatibility, while others would interpret it as temporarily not having time to verify. Neither interpretation is suitable for handoff.

Therefore, the approved scope is the evidence scope, not the organizational scope. An object belongs to the portion that can be continued this round only when the result observed by caller Fang Ke and the same-entry counterexample have both been included in the assessment. The remaining objects retain their original status and await separate technical review.

## Rejected Options and Reasons

We did not adopt the option to "switch the window first and restore it if a problem occurs." This option treats withdrawal as a routine operation without first fixing what phenomenon triggers the withdrawal. Recovery without explicit conditions leaves the judgment to the person on duty's immediate interpretation, making different handling likely after the rotation.

We also did not adopt the option to "have on-call personnel continue following up on every unresolved item." It mixes preserving the live context with technical judgment, guarantees neither that the reproduction entry point is usable nor that the person taking over understands the caller impact sufficiently. On-call can continue maintaining status, but cannot replace the review by the module owner, QA, or interface maintainer.

Finally, we did not turn a single observation in chat directly into a global rule. Conclusions about cross-package behavior must return to the result observed by caller Fang Ke and check the same-entry counterexample. A local reproduction is enough to remind us to pause the candidate path, but not enough to make a judgment for all callers.

## Processing Order During Handoff

When an item requiring continued handling during the freeze is received, first confirm whether it still uses the current mutation-runtime entry point. If so, check whether the owner, reproduction entry point, and withdrawal conditions in the record are complete. Items with all three can carry their original scope into the rotation; items with missing pieces remain pending confirmation, and the missing content becomes input for the next technical review.

If the item is a window-adjustment candidate, do not mix it into the routine handoff for the current entry point. Record separately the proposed path change, the result callers can observe, the known counterexamples, and the withdrawal action. Only when these contents correspond to the actual technical review can we reconsider whether the item should enter the release scope.

If a counterexample appears during review, prioritize withdrawing the candidate path; do not cover the counterexample with a temporary explanation. Then preserve the entry point corresponding to the counterexample for use in the next judgment. The goal during the freeze is not to close every issue immediately, but to avoid changing a path already in use when the judgment cannot be repeated.

## Relationship to Build Queue Handoff

The switch handoff maintained by the build queue is documented separately in DOC-52. The two sets of materials share the handoff threshold: when any of the consumer, entry point, current decision maker, or withdrawal action is missing, do not record the switch as complete. They do not share technical conclusions; this record handles only entry-point selection under on-call rotation and the release freeze.

## Reservations

Window adjustment remains valuable, but there is currently no reason to disguise it as a completed release change. If the observed results for caller Fang Ke, the same-entry counterexample, and the withdrawal action are filled in later, it can be proposed again; until then, the current mutation-runtime entry point is the only path that will continue to be used through this round's rotation.

Another issue that has not yet been split out is whether multiple unresolved items pointing to the same caller entry point may share one minimum reproduction. The current decision requires only that a reproduction entry point exist; it does not specify under what conditions a shared entry point is sufficient to cover different items. This issue does not affect the decision to retain the entry point this round, but it should not be misread as already resolved.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Unresolved item during freeze] --> B{owner, entry point, and withdrawal conditions all present}
  B -->|Yes| C[Handoff along current entry point]
  B -->|No| D[Remain pending confirmation]
  C --> E{Same-entry counterexample appears}
  E -->|Yes| F[Withdraw candidate path]
  E -->|No| G[Retain original scope]
```

# Build Queue Cutover Handoff Guide

Do not treat the build queue as fully migrated in this cutover. The handoff covers known consumers in the monorepo associated with solid-adapter, along with the legacy entry points those consumers still use. Get a complete count of both first, then choose one consumer that can be rolled back independently to try the candidate path.

Follow this handoff sequence.

1. List the known consumers. Include only consumers confirmed to be connected to solid-adapter; do not pad the list with similarly named packages. Note the legacy entry point each consumer currently uses beside its name.
2. Choose one consumer from the list that can be rolled back independently. Route only this consumer through the candidate path first, so the queue cutover and differences among multiple consumers do not get folded into a single assessment.
3. Provide the public entry point and a minimal reproduction. The person taking over should be able to get back to the same candidate path from that entry point and see the result this trial is meant to verify; "tested" without an entry point is not sufficient for handoff.
4. Name the current owner. The reporter is responsible for recording what happened and updating the status, not signing off on the implementation. Technical confirmation is provided by the relevant module owner, QA, or interface maintainer; someone forwarding information does not mean the review is complete.
5. Document the rollback action. If the candidate path produces unacceptable results, the consumer should be able to return to the legacy entry point. If the rollback action is not clearly documented, keep the page marked as migration in progress; do not mark the cutover complete.

The handoff package should include at least: known consumers and their legacy entry points, the trial consumer, the public entry point, a minimal reproduction, the current owner, and the rollback action. Until all callers have been counted, you can keep working on the list, but do not expand the candidate path prematurely; if the rollback action is still undecided, do not leave subsequent on-call staff to decide how to roll back from memory on the spot.

If the trial consumer needs to return to the legacy entry point after the cutover, first carry out the documented rollback action, then add what you observed to the handoff record. Do not interpret a single rollback as meaning that none of the consumers can migrate; it only shows that this candidate path cannot yet replace the legacy entry point. The other known consumers remain on the list, waiting until they each meet the conditions for a trial and rollback.

DOC-53 records the actual entry points for the cross-framework compatibility window. This guide does not substitute for its assessment of framework behavior; it only records who is using which path during the build queue cutover, who can confirm it, and how to return to the legacy entry point.

## On-Call Handoff Checks

The person taking over should first choose a consumer from the list that still uses the legacy entry point, rerun the recorded minimal reproduction, and put the start time, actual result, and rollback entry point on the same line. If the result differs from the handoff package, keep the status as migration in progress; do not switch to a different consumer on the spot just to get a green result.

Then verify that the owner can still handle that module. If only the reporter is online and the technical owner is absent, you can update the observations, but you cannot close the cutover item. If you need to hand it off to QA or the interface maintainer, include the original entry point, candidate path, and the result you just obtained so the person taking over does not have to guess the scope again.

Finally, run a rollback drill: leave the other consumers in the queue unchanged, return only the trial consumer to the legacy entry point, and confirm that the original record is still accessible. If the observation conditions have changed after the rollback, create a new record describing the differences rather than overwriting the handoff baseline on this page. The person taking over is responsible for posting the drill results back to the original card.

The handoff provides the public entry point, minimal reproduction, current owner, and rollback action, and does not let nontechnical roles sign off on behalf of the implementers." framework-exports
        |

integrations/react-next/next.config.js
        |
        v
One direct caller
        |
        v
First real consumer of the cross-framework compatibility window
